title: Evaporative demand did not cause the post-1997 runoff loss in 175 south-east Australian catchments or start the offset in 260 eastern US catchments; after 2009 it explains about half of the US offset
abstract: Question: after 1997, runoff in south-east Australia (SE-AU, 175 catchments) fell below the 1951-1996 rainfall-runoff relation with a loss of rain response, and runoff in the eastern US (East-US, 260 catchments) fell by a constant offset. Does an increase of atmospheric evaporative demand cause these shifts? Approach: we fixed a plan before any demand result. We used CRU TS 4.09 PET, CAMELS-AUS SILO pan, Morton and FAO-56 series, and GHCN-Daily station pans. Per catchment we fitted the Fu (Budyko) parameter to 1951-1996 means and predicted 1997-2009 and 2010-end runoff from rain only and from rain plus PET. Results: in SE-AU the rain-only deficit was -52 and -56 mm/yr. Demand explained 10-26% of it in 1997-2009 with all four products and -12% to 31% in 2010-2021; SILO Morton PET and pan evaporation did not increase after 2009 (-0.2%, -1.7%), and residuals were least negative in high-demand years (r = +0.68). In the East-US, the deficit started in 1997-2009 (-23 mm/yr) while CRU PET was 0.7% lower than before (CI -1.2 to -0.2%); station pans rose 2.5% (CI -0.7 to 5.6%). After 2009 CRU PET rose 4.1% and explains 49% (CI 35-82%) of the -30 mm/yr deficit; a non-demand offset of -15 to -26 mm/yr remains. Within the East-US, catchments with larger PET increases did not have larger deficits (Spearman +0.09). Conclusion: demand is not the cause of the SE-AU loss and did not start the East-US offset; after 2009 it can explain about half of the East-US offset. Limitations: demand products disagree, the US pan network is small, the fixed-parameter Budyko frame has placebo biases of 8-19 mm/yr, and demand is not actual ET.
